idiom_name: empty module included into a class, tested with is_a?
implementation_notes: Ruby modules are the language's marker mechanism: define an empty module, include it into a class (or extend it into an object), and test with is_a?/kind_of?; inclusion adds the type relationship and nothing else, which is exactly the classic structure with no extra machinery. Ruby's culture prefers duck typing (respond_to?) for behaviour, so use a tag module when a nominal fact must be recognised across unrelated classes - persistence strategies, serialization, enumeration - and document the consumer. Keep tag modules empty; if they declare methods they stop being markers.
code_sketch:
module Deletable; end          # empty tag module

class Order
  include Deletable
end

Order.new.is_a?(Deletable)     # => true
pitfalls: include also runs the module's included hook and brings its constants; keep tag modules empty or name the hook's effect explicitly.
is_a? walks ancestors, so every subclass and including class inherits the tag and cannot drop it.
An empty module reads as an accident unless a comment names the consumer. Document what checks the tag.

variants.name: Per-object tagging via the singleton class
variants.idiom_name: obj.extend(Tag) adding the module to one object only
variants.implementation_notes: obj.extend(Tag) adds the module to just that object's singleton class, so individual instances of the same class can carry different marks and obj.is_a?(Tag) distinguishes them; this is the Ruby way to express per-instance capabilities such as a deletable row. The mark lives on the singleton class, so clone keeps it and dup does not. Use it sparingly - per-object tags defeat class-level documentation and can upset frameworks that assume uniform instances.
variants.code_sketch:
module Deletable; end

row = Shape.new
row.extend(Deletable)

row.is_a?(Deletable)           # => true for this instance only
Shape.new.is_a?(Deletable)     # => false
pitfalls: dup drops singleton-class members while clone keeps them, so copied objects can silently lose the tag.
Per-object tags are invisible in the class definition, which makes them hard to discover and document.
Extending an object mutates its singleton class, which some concurrency models and serializers cannot share or persist.
